data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["HTTP idempotency keys are typically server-enforced, whereas event-log deduplication may be writer-side or consumer-side"],"overturn_conditions":["If HTTP safety is defined purely in terms of client-observable effects while event-log safety is defined in terms of infrastructure integrity, the two frameworks use 'safe' for different concepts and the analogy breaks down.","If the relevant published definitions come from distributed-systems literature rather than HTTP semantics, the HTTP-based distinction between safe and idempotent may not map cleanly onto event-log terminology."],"shared_structure":["Both HTTP and event logs involve operations that may be retried by the transport layer","Both distinguish between 'no side effects' (safe) and 'same effect on retry' (idempotent)","Both must handle duplicate delivery at the application or infrastructure boundary"],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_005"],"transfer_claims":["If an operation produces a necessary side effect (log append / server state change), safety (no side effects) is the wrong property to require; idempotency (same effect on retry) is the correct requirement.","The transport layer may deliver the same operation multiple times; the application or infrastructure boundary must recognize duplicates and collapse them to a single effect.","Requiring idempotency does not eliminate the side effect but constrains its replay behavior, analogous to how PUT in HTTP is idempotent despite mutating server state."]},"claim":"Drawing on HTTP semantics (RFC 7231) as a candidate published definition source: 'safe' methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) are defined as having no side effects on server state, while 'idempotent' methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) are defined as having the same intended effect regardless of call count. For an append-only event log, the correct requirement is idempotency, not safety, because writing to the log IS a side effect\u2014it must be controlled to produce the same result on retry, not eliminated entirely.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the published definitions referenced by the problem are not HTTP semantics but database or distributed systems literature, this mapping may not hold.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'safe' in the relevant literature is defined differently from HTTP's definition (no side effects), the distinction shifts.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the problem's context treats append as inherently side-effect-free at the logical level (events are immutable facts, not mutations), then safety and idempotency may converge.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"In HTTP terms, a log writer is analogous to a client issuing PUT requests: the side effect (appending to the log) is intended and necessary, so safety (no side effects) is the wrong property. Idempotency (same effect on retry) is correct: the writer's append must produce the same log state whether attempted once or multiple times, which requires deduplication at the writer or log level, analogous to an HTTP server recognizing idempotent-method retries.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
